newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: New Karachi index helps Pakistan stocks surge.
newsitem.headline: New Karachi index helps Pakistan stocks surge.

text.p: The Karachi 100-share share price index has jumped more than eight percent since a recomposed version made its debut on July 1, but analysts say that prospects for further climbs are limited.

The Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) index has gained some 10 percent in six successive sessions to Tuesday mainly on rises in Pakistan Telecommunication Co. Ltd (PTCL) and Hub Power shares, which together constitute more than 42 percent of the new index's weight.
Analysts said the re-formed index was unlikely to shoot beyond the 1,850-point level.
Almost all blue chips posted handsome gains in the recent rally, but 72 percent of the index's rise was due to Hub Power and PTCL, said a research note by SocGen-Crosby Securities.
IF PTCL SNEEZES, MARKET WILL CATCH COLD

"The new index is heavily skewed towards PTCL, which comprises 30.64 percent of the index weight," SocGen Crosby said. "The top three companies -- PTCL, Hub Power and Pakistan State Oil -- constitute about 50 percent of the index."
It said PTCL and Hub Power would set market direction, making the index highly susceptible to their price movements.
A one-rupee rise in PTCL would move the index 15.3 points. A similar rise in Hub Power would lift it 4.7 points, it added.

"With our estimate of PTCL's fair value at 36 rupees ($0.89) a share and Hub Power at 53, it would be extremely difficult for the index to break the 1,850 level even if other share prices rose by 20 percent," the research note said.
Ather Raouf, director of sales at Carr Mashriq, also felt the market was now too dependent on PTCL. "The recomposed index has increased the market's volatility," he said.
He said PTCL was fundamentally a weak company and had only a limited upside from current levels.
Asghar Merchant of KASB & Co said PTCL's performance would be more important than ever for the Karachi index.
"PTCL has to perform well and show sustainable strength to boost the market, though its track record shows it has slightly underperformed the market," he said.
He said foreigners interested in Pakistan look primarily at PTCL and Hub Power scrips because of their adequate liquidity and availability through Global Depository Receipts.
Merchant said the 1997/98 (July-June) budget had improved PTCL's prospects by cutting excise duty and trunk call charges.
Nadeem Naqvi, chief analyst at International Asset Management Company, said index-linked funds would raise their holding in PTCL because of its increased index weighting.
"There is also serious interest in Hub Power after its problem of payments with WAPDA (the state-owned Water and Power Development Authority) has been removed," he said.

Hub Power said in June that WAPDA had failed to supply a letter of credit required under the terms of a power purchase agreement. "This problem, as expected, has now been solved. It has reassured investors about the stock's strength," Naqvi said.
FINALLY, SIGNS OF NEW INVESTMENT
He said that after a long absence, serious investment was coming in from index and hedge funds and the base of the market would rise from 1,350 points or so to 1,600 points.
"The present rally is the firming-up of the market and it will stabilise at around the 1,650-point level," Naqvi added.
Analysts said economic fundamentals were the most important factor in sustaining recent gains in the mid- to long-term. Otherwise the index would plunge as fast as it has risen.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government, trying to revive the economy, has launched a bold programme of structural reforms, spending cuts and measures to boost exports.

"The direction of the government's economic policies is right, but it will take time for the reforms to make an impact," Naqvi said, adding that the government's revenue targets were optimistic, whereas its spending targets seemed realistic.
"Like neighbouring India, Pakistan's government is striving for stable economic policies," Naqvi said.
"These steps may not give quick and high dividends as they did in India because our economy is in a much worse condition, but eventually they will pull it out of its current lows."
INVESTOR CONFIDENCE STILL FRAGILE

Naqvi said government measures had restored some confidence to wary investors, who had seen only a downward trend for the past three years. "They don't believe that a turn-round is around the corner and are often short sellers at high levels.

"Last month's default of MRJ's Securities is also linked to this fact. It has made jobbers hesitant to short-sell which is good," he said, referring to the KSE's action in cancelling the membership of M. Rashid Jamal's MRJ Securities for defaulting on share transactions worth more than 80 million rupees.
Merchant said foreign funds would not enter Pakistan aggressively until the International Monetary Fund approves a new medium-term lending programme to back economic reforms.
"Much depends on the Pakistan-IMF talks this month. There won't be any inflow of foreign investment until the government manages to get an ESAF (enhanced structural adjustment facility)," he said.
An IMF mission was due in Islamabad on Wednesday to start talks on a new ESAF, but Raza Mirza, chief analyst of KASB & Co, said it was too early to expect any breakthrough.
